chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Yusuf ibn Aqil from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'That the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) ruled regarding

the 'Umra' (life estate): 'That it is valid for the one who established it. So whoever establishes something, as long as he is alive, it belongs to him; and when he dies, it belongs to his heirs.' This does not contradict what we have previously stated, because his saying (peace be upon him) 'it belongs to his heirs when he dies' means the one for whom the 'Umra was established (the beneficiary), not the one who established it. And if he meant the one who established it, he would not have said 'it belongs to his heirs,' because when he dies, the 'Umra returns to the one who established it, if he is alive, or to his heirs, if he is dead, according to what we have stated previously. Unless he makes it for him and his children and his descendants, as long as any of them remain, as we have clarified.

key_terms.أَعْمَرَهَا: He established it (as a life estate)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on 'Umra (life estate) in Shia jurisprudence and who inherits the property after the owner's death?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), transmitted via the chain of Muhammad ibn Qays, clarifies the default legal presumption in Shia jurisprudence that 'Umra (life estate) is a temporary usufruct for the grantor unless explicitly designated as permanent for the beneficiary. It highlights the scholarly distinction between the grantor's retained ownership and the beneficiary's limited right, ensuring that upon death, the property reverts to the grantor's heirs, a nuance critical for understanding inheritance laws in classical texts like Tahdhib al-Ahkam.
